newsitem.title: USA: Investor lawyer pleased with High Court on Denver.
newsitem.headline: Investor lawyer pleased with High Court on Denver.

text.p: A lawyer for Denver International Airport bondholders said Monday she is pleased that the U.S. Supreme Court opted not to hear an appeal over bondholders' rights to sue cities.

The High Court issued a curt statement at 1000 EDT Monday denying the city and county of Denver's request that it review a November 1996 appeals court decision not to block bondholders from suing the localities over $3 billion of Denver International Airport bonds.

"I'm glad. But I expected it," bondholders' lawyer Sherrie Savett said in a telephone interview. Denver's case represented an "extremely strained" interpretation of the federal securities laws, Savett said.

The city had argued that while amendments to the securities laws passed by Congress in 1975 make clear that the Securities and Exchange Commission can sue municipalities for securities fraud violations, that 1975 language does not explicity say private entities can sue.
Denver attorneys also had argued that cities are agents of states and therefore have constitutional immunity from such court actions.

But Savett said, "That immunity is only extended to states. And here, it was the city of Denver that was responsible for these bonds. The prospectuses specifically stated that the state of Colorado had no financial responsibility," Savett said.
James Lyons, an attorney for Denver, was unavailable for comment.

The original lawsuit filed over two years ago by Bonnie Sonnenfeld and other Denver airport bonds charged that Denver knew, but failed to disclose, problems with a state-of-the-art baggage handling system.
The problems triggered an 18-month delay in the airport's opening and a downgrade of the bonds' ratings.
The bondholders' lawsuit is pending in U.S. district court.
